prompt: The question is "which ten states buy the most?" Which chart answers it best?

choices.text: A choropleth map of the states
choices.why: A map shows patterns by place; it ranks poorly because colour is low on the ladder.

choices.text: A map with a circle on every state
choices.why: Circle areas are read short, so close ranks blur.

choices.text: A pie with ten slices and an other slice
choices.why: Eleven slices is far beyond what a pie does well.

choices.text: A sorted bar chart
choices.why: Right. A ranking is position and length, above any colour.

prompt: On a map, why must the number go into colour or symbol size?

choices.text: Geography takes position
choices.why: Right. The two best channels say where each place is.

choices.text: Maps cannot show numbers any other way, by convention of cartographers
choices.why: It is not convention; it is that position is used up.

choices.text: Colour is the most accurate channel
choices.why: Colour is near the bottom of the ladder.

choices.text: Readers prefer colourful maps
choices.why: Preference is not the reason.

prompt: Why does Amazonas tend to dominate a shaded map of Brazil, whatever its value?

choices.text: It has the most people
choices.why: São Paulo has far more people.

choices.text: It covers far more of the page
choices.why: Right. The eye weighs a colour by how much area it covers.

choices.text: Its colour is always the strongest
choices.why: Its colour depends on its value, which here is low.

choices.text: It sits at the top of the map, where readers look first
choices.why: Its size, not its position, is what dominates.

prompt: What does a choropleth of total orders by state mostly show?

choices.text: Where Horta does best
choices.why: That needs a rate, orders per person.

choices.text: Where deliveries are fastest
choices.why: Orders say nothing about delivery speed.

choices.text: Where people live
choices.why: Right. Any count tracks population.

choices.text: Which states are growing
choices.why: Growth needs two periods.

prompt: The Federal District had 5,480 orders and 2.8 million people. How many orders per thousand people is that, to two decimal places?
A map should show where late deliveries are a problem. What should each state be shaded by?

choices.text: The number of late deliveries
choices.why: A count would mostly show where the orders are.

choices.text: The area of the state
choices.why: Area has nothing to do with lateness.

choices.text: The number of drivers
choices.why: That is another count, and not the question.

choices.text: The share of its orders delivered late
choices.why: Right. A share is a rate, so big states do not win by size.

prompt: With equal-interval classes, 21 of the 27 states fell into the two lowest classes. What did the map look like?

choices.text: Mostly pale
choices.why: Right, with a single state in the top class.

choices.text: Evenly spread across the shades
choices.why: That is what quantiles produce.

choices.text: Mostly in the strongest shade
choices.why: The opposite: most states were in the low classes.

choices.text: Identical to the quantile map
choices.why: The two methods gave very different pictures.

prompt: What do quantile classes guarantee?

choices.text: Classes of equal width
choices.why: That is equal intervals.

choices.text: Breaks in the largest gaps between values
choices.why: That is natural breaks, also called Jenks.

choices.text: About the same number of places in each class
choices.why: Right, which uses every shade and can split near-identical values.

choices.text: Round numbers for every break
choices.why: Quantile breaks fall wherever the data puts them.

prompt: Two maps compare the rate by state in 2024 and 2025, each with quantile breaks computed from its own year. What is wrong?

choices.text: Quantiles cannot be used for rates
choices.why: They can; the problem is changing them between maps.

choices.text: Two maps should never be compared
choices.why: They can be, with the same breaks.

choices.text: Each year has its own breaks, so a shade means different rates in the two
choices.why: Right. Use the same breaks for both, or the comparison is between methods.

choices.text: Rates should be counts for a comparison over time
choices.why: Counts would bring back the population problem.

prompt: How should total orders appear on a map?

choices.text: As a shade on each state
choices.why: Shading by count mostly shows population.

choices.text: As circles sized by radius
choices.why: That squares the differences.

choices.text: As circles sized by area
choices.why: Right. The count goes on a symbol, not on a shade.

choices.text: As the state's label in a larger font
choices.why: Font size is a poor channel for a number.

prompt: Why are the states in the symbol map drawn in one neutral grey?

choices.text: Because grey prints cheaply
choices.why: Cost is not the reason.

choices.text: Because colour is reserved for the legend
choices.why: The legend describes the circles, not the reason for grey.

choices.text: To hide the states with no orders
choices.why: Every state has orders, and every state is still drawn.

choices.text: So the state's size does not compete with the circles
choices.why: Right. Only the symbols carry the data.

prompt: A dot density map puts one dot per 100 orders inside each state, at random positions. What might a reader wrongly conclude?

choices.text: That the totals are wrong
choices.why: The number of dots is right; their positions are not real.

choices.text: That every state has the same number of orders
choices.why: The density of dots varies, which is the point.

choices.text: That the map uses an equal-area projection
choices.why: Dots say nothing about the projection.

choices.text: That a dot marks a real address
choices.why: Right. The positions inside an area are invented.

prompt: What does the Mercator projection keep, and what does it inflate?

choices.text: Keeps areas, squashes shapes
choices.why: That is an equal-area projection.

choices.text: Keeps local shapes, inflates areas towards the poles
choices.why: Right. At 60 degrees, areas are four times what they are at the equator.

choices.text: Keeps both shapes and areas
choices.why: No flat map keeps both.

choices.text: Keeps distances, inflates angles
choices.why: Mercator keeps angles, not distances.

prompt: On Mercator a small circle's width grows by 1 ÷ cos(latitude). How many times its equator area does it have at 60 degrees?
hint: cos 60° is 0.5, and both directions stretch.

prompt: Which projection fits a world choropleth of a rate?

choices.text: Web Mercator
choices.why: It inflates high latitudes, so Canada and Russia dominate.

choices.text: Any, since colour does not depend on area
choices.why: The eye weighs colour by area, so it does.

choices.text: Equal Earth
choices.why: Right. Equal-area, so each country's colour weighs what its area does.

choices.text: The one the tool uses by default, whatever it is
choices.why: Defaults are usually Mercator.

prompt: What does a tile map give every place?

choices.text: Its true shape
choices.why: Tile maps give up shape.

choices.text: The same weight
choices.why: Right. One equal square each.

choices.text: A size by its population
choices.why: That would be a cartogram.

choices.text: Its exact borders with every neighbour
choices.why: A grid cannot keep every adjacency.

prompt: When is a cartogram a poor choice?

choices.text: When the data is a count
choices.why: Counts are exactly what cartograms resize by.

choices.text: When the map has more than ten areas
choices.why: The number of areas is not the issue.

choices.text: When the areas differ in size
choices.why: That is when a cartogram helps most.

choices.text: When the audience does not know the real map well
choices.why: Right. A bent map nobody recognises needs the real one beside it.

prompt: This tile map shades Brazil's states by orders per thousand people, from faint to strong. Find each of these.

labels.text: the state with the highest rate

hint: The strongest square sits in the middle of the country.

prompt: Match each map to what it carries.

pairs.right: a rate, as a shade on each area
a count, as a circle's area
a count, as many small dots
a value, as the size of the area itself

right_distractors: a count, as a shade on each area
